_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a4.1: And furthermore, if it is so: that we expound an a fortiori inference regarding animals, then the Levites should be exempt from the firstborn of a kosher animal too, since their own kosher animals abrogated [the firstborn status of] the Israelites’ animals.
rashi:a4.2: Why did we learn, etc.: in the second chapter (13a below).
rashi:a5.1: Rather, Rava said: regarding animals the Rabbis did not expound an a fortiori inference, since the Torah had to juxtapose the firstborn of a non-kosher animal to the firstborn of man, [teaching that] anything that does not apply to the firstborn of man does not apply to the firstborn of a non-kosher animal, as below. Learn from this that regarding animals this a fortiori inference was not given to be expounded. And this is what the mishna is saying: priests and Levites are themselves exempt from the redemption of the son, by an a fortiori inference.
rashi:a5.2: If [the sanctity of the Levites] abrogated: if the sanctity of the ordinary [non-firstborn] Levites abrogated the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn in the wilderness, it is logical that the sanctity of the firstborn among them should be abrogated; as is said below, the firstborn Levites abrogated only themselves.
rashi:a6.1: From where do we derive a non-kosher animal: that priests are exempt from [redeeming] the firstborn donkey.
rashi:a6.2: Anything that does not apply to the firstborn of man: such as Levites and priests, who are exempt by the a fortiori inference.
rashi:a7.1: According to you, who say their animals: since you expound the a fortiori inference for animals too.
rashi:a7.2: A Levite who had a lamb: in the wilderness, which abrogated the firstborn donkeys that were there in the wilderness.
rashi:a8.1: Both according to you and according to Rava: who [both] expound an a fortiori inference regarding the human firstborn. Since you expound it for animals, all the more so for people; for if you did not expound an a fortiori inference there, from where would we derive it for a person? And since you expound it, one can challenge: a firstborn Levite a month old [should be exempt], since we find that an ordinary Levite a month old abrogated the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn, for all of them were counted from a month old and upward, as it is written (Numbers 3:15): “from a month old and upward.” Let the firstborn himself be abrogated: it is logical that firstborn Levites a month old exempt themselves by an a fortiori inference from the ordinary ones a month old, who abrogated the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn; all the more so those a month old themselves.
rashi:a8.2: A firstborn less than a month old, who did not abrogate: since an ordinary [Levite] of his age did not abrogate the sanctity of an Israelite firstborn, let his own sanctity not be abrogated. Then why were the firstborn Levites in the wilderness who were less than a month old not redeemed with money?
rashi:a9.1: A female Levite who gave birth: [from an] Israelite: the firstborn status of her son should not be abrogated, since in the wilderness only males were counted, and the females abrogated nothing.
rashi:a10.1: The Merciful One made it depend on the firstborn of the womb: [made] the firstborn [depend on it]. Since the womb is that of this Levite woman, we follow the mother with regard to the five sela. If we find that all the Levites are exempt, even those less than a month old who were in the wilderness, [who did not abrogate anything,] then the son of a Levite woman is exempt too.
rashi:a11.1: And Aaron, who was not in that count: neither he nor his animals, which did not abrogate the Israelite firstborn; so his firstborn donkeys should not be abrogated.
rashi:a12.1: Were juxtaposed, etc.: now all the challenges are resolved.
tosafot:a2.1: It is only logical that it should abrogate their own: this is the reading [shetafki’a et, with the object marker “et”]; one who reads shetipaka [“that it be abrogated”] does not read “et”.
tosafot:a3.1: But doesn’t it teach “they rendered exempt”: from the first clause, which teaches “and the priests and Levites are exempt,” there is no difficulty at all, since one could explain it to mean that they are exempt from sanctifying their firstborn donkeys, not that they themselves are exempt. But “they rendered exempt” implies that they themselves rendered exempt.
tosafot:a4.1: And furthermore, if it is so: that we expound an a fortiori inference regarding animals, the Levites should be exempt from the firstborn of a kosher animal, since their animals abrogated the Israelites’ kosher animals. And if you say: if so, below, where [Rabbi Ḥanina] says that one lamb of a Levite exempted several firstborn donkeys of an Israelite, why did he not mention a kosher animal? For one cannot say that with kosher animals one lamb did not exempt several kosher firstborn of the Israelites, and that only with firstborn donkeys [did one exempt many], while for kosher animals they counted one against one: since what the Levites’ animals exempted of the Israelites’, whether non-kosher or kosher, he derives from “the animal [of the Levites] in exchange for their animals,” and from that he derives below “one animal in exchange for many animals,” which implies both non-kosher and kosher. One can answer: Rabbi Ḥanina below mentions what can still apply now. And furthermore, one can explain that the mishna below comes [to say]: what is the reason one redeems and redeems again? Because one lamb of a Levite exempted several firstborn donkeys of an Israelite in the wilderness. But that one Levite lamb in the wilderness exempted several kosher firstborn of an Israelite applied only at that time, since now they have no redemption but have sanctity of the body. And if you say: what does Abaye hold, and why does he not make the a fortiori inference for a kosher animal? One can answer: he holds that regarding kosher animals, which have sanctity for the altar, it does not fit to say that they exempt their own by an a fortiori inference from exempting the Israelites’, since priests and Levites are closer to the altar than Israelites.
tosafot:a5.1: In brief: Tosafot ask what kind of a fortiori inference this is, since it was the ordinary Levites who abrogated the Israelite firstborn, while the firstborn Levites abrogated nothing (as below); how then can one argue to the firstborn Levites? They answer, as Rashi explained, that the inference rests on Levite status: if a Levite’s Levite status abrogated the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn, then a firstborn Levite’s own Levite status should surely abrogate his own. That is why it says below that a firstborn does not abrogate a firstborn: a Levite’s status cannot abrogate two firstborn statuses, his own and an Israelite’s. They then ask why Rava rejects Abaye’s inference for animals, which seems a sound one. Rashi’s reason, that the Torah had to juxtapose the firstborn of a non-kosher animal to the firstborn of man (“anything that does not apply to the firstborn of man…”), which shows that no a fortiori inference was given for animals, does not fit the wording: “We have found man; from where do we derive a non-kosher animal?” implies the juxtaposition is needed to teach about the non-kosher animal, not to show that one may not reason about the kosher one. Besides, the juxtaposition may be needed for the derivation below that for a non-kosher animal one does not distinguish between later generations and that time [both with a lamb], from which one also learns that one may redeem again and again with one lamb; and Rabbi Eliezer needs it at the end of the chapter (12b): just as one bears responsibility for the firstborn of man, so for the firstborn of a non-kosher animal. Tosafot propose instead: only for a person, where Levite sanctity is what causes the abrogation of firstborn status, does an a fortiori inference fit; for an animal, where the Levites’ lamb has no sanctity that causes the abrogation, it does not. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a5.2: It is only logical that it abrogate his own: Rashi explained that according to Rava, “exempt” in the mishna refers to the redemption of the son. That is difficult, since we are dealing with the firstborn donkey. Rabbeinu Tam explained that the mishna means: priests and Levites are exempt from redeeming the firstborn donkey. What is the reason? Since they themselves are exempt by an a fortiori inference, therefore we learn the non-kosher animal from its juxtaposition to man. But the wording “this is what it is saying” is somewhat difficult on this explanation.
tosafot:a7.1: One who did not have a lamb that would abrogate, let them not be abrogated: And if you say: there is still an a fortiori inference either way: if a Levite’s lamb exempted the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys, all the more so those of other Levites who had no lamb! One can answer that this is not an a fortiori inference: the verse did not say to take the animal of this Levite in exchange for the animal of another Levite, but in exchange for the Israelites’ animals. Still, for his own [animals], when he has [a lamb], we make the a fortiori inference.
tosafot:a8.1: One a month old, who abrogated, let him be abrogated: it does not mean that a firstborn Levite a month old, who abrogated an Israelite firstborn, should have [his own status] abrogated, since a firstborn does not abrogate a firstborn. Rather, it means: one a month old, whose Levite status has the power to abrogate Israelite firstborn [status], should have his own firstborn status abrogated, since an ordinary Levite like him abrogates Israelite firstborn; but one who was less than a month old at that time should not have his own firstborn status abrogated, even though afterward he became a month old. And the same for firstborn from then on: since at that time [Levite status] did not abrogate, so too for later generations, as is expounded shortly: “and they shall be,” they shall remain as they were.
tosafot:a10.1: The Merciful One made it depend on the firstborn of the womb: Rashi explained: since the womb is that of this Levite woman, if we find that all the Levites are exempt, even those less than a month old who were in the wilderness, the son of a Levite woman is exempt too. This implies that he leaves this challenge, [the son of the Levite woman,] to the answer “firstborn of the womb” together with the [challenge of the] Levite less than a month old, [awaiting] the answer “all the Levites were juxtaposed to each other.” That does not seem right; rather, it is fully answered by “firstborn of the womb.” [Like] a Levite less than a month old, he has no deficiency other than that [his mother was not counted], and he is the son of a Levite [woman]; and since the Merciful One made it depend on the womb, his being a Levite’s son makes him a Levite, even though his father is not a Levite. [The Hebrew here is compressed; our brackets follow the sense of the argument.]
tosafot:a11.1: And Aaron, who was not in that count: Rashi explained: neither he nor his animals, which did not abrogate the Israelite firstborn, so his firstborn [donkeys] should not be abrogated. This implies that he does not mean to ask as well that Aaron’s own firstborn status should not be abrogated; and indeed one cannot say that, since Aaron was not a firstborn: Miriam was three years older than him, as the Midrash says [at the beginning of Shemot], just as Aaron was three years older than Moses. And if you say: why is Aaron more of a difficulty than the three hundred firstborn Levites who were not counted among the twenty-two thousand, as below? One can answer: although they were not counted toward the twenty-two thousand, since it is enough for a firstborn to abrogate himself, they were still counted in the census of the Levites; but Aaron was not counted at all.
gershom:a1.1: A person, a person rendered exempt: a Levite exempted an Israelite human firstborn, and their animals, [that is,] their sheep, exempted the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys, as it is written: “Take the Levites in exchange for all the firstborn,” etc.
gershom:a2.1: Abaye said, this is what it is saying [a gloss suggests the text should read: “explain the mishna thus: priests and Levites are exempt,” etc.]: their animals are exempt by an a fortiori inference: if their animals abrogated, etc. And the same holds for Abaye: they themselves, who abrogated the Israelite firstborn, should by right abrogate the firstborn of their own sons.
gershom:a3.1: Rava said to him: how can you explain it as “if [their] animals abrogated”? But it teaches “they rendered exempt” [pateru], not “it rendered exempt” [patra], which implies that the mishna speaks of them themselves.
gershom:a4.1: And furthermore, if it is so: that it teaches that their animals rendered exempt, as you say, they should be exempt from the firstborn of a kosher animal too. Why did we learn: they were not exempted, etc.? Because it is written: “Yet you shall redeem the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of the kosher animal you shall redeem.” [So Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the verse, Numbers 18:15, reads “non-kosher animal”.]
gershom:a5.1: Rather, Rava said, this is what it is saying, etc.: We have found man: that firstborn Levites are exempt by an a fortiori inference, as we said.
gershom:a6.1: The firstborn of a non-kosher animal: that priests and Levites are exempt from it, from where do we derive it?
gershom:a7.1: The verse states, “Yet,” etc. Anything that applies to the firstborn of man: such as an Israelite, who must redeem him, applies to the firstborn donkey too, which he must redeem.
gershom:a8.1: And anything that does not apply to the firstborn of man: [such as Levites,] who as we said are exempt by the a fortiori inference, are also exempt from redeeming the firstborn of a non-kosher animal.
gershom:a9.1: Rav Safra said to Abaye: according to you, who said “if their animals abrogated,” etc.: if so, a Levite who had a lamb that abrogated an Israelite’s firstborn donkey, let his own firstborn donkey be abrogated, that is, be exempt, since it exempted the Israelite’s; and one who did not have a lamb that abrogated, let his own not be abrogated either.
gershom:a10.1: Both according to you and according to Rava: even Abaye, who said “if [their] animals abrogated,” also holds that the Levites themselves abrogated the sanctity of the Israelite firstborn. And he says to him: if so, by your reasoning, one a month old, as it is written “from a month old and upward,” who abrogated, let him be abrogated, so that his firstborn [status] is exempt.
gershom:a11.1: A Levite woman too, who did not abrogate, since “every male” is written: her firstborn [son’s status] should not be abrogated. Why then does Rav [Adda] say, etc.
gershom:a12.1: As he says: The Merciful One made it depend on the firstborn of the womb. That is, we do not assign her son to [his father, an] Israelite, but to her, since the Merciful One made it depend on the womb. And she is of the tribe that is exempt from firstborn status: had she been a male and a firstborn, she would have been exempt; so her son too, who comes from that womb, is exempt, as she would have been exempt from firstborn status had she been a male.
gershom:a13.1: And Aaron, who was not in the count of the twenty-two thousand Levites: his firstborn in the wilderness should not be abrogated, since he did not abrogate.
gershom:a14.1: Why are there dots over “Aaron” in the book of Numbers: as it is written, “All the redeemed of the Levites, whom Moses and Aaron and his sons numbered” [so Rabbeinu Gershom quotes Numbers 3:39]: that he was not in that count, since every dot comes to exclude.
gershom:a15.1: All the Levites were juxtaposed to each other: just as one a month old, who exempted, has his firstborn [status] exempt, so one less than a month old, who did not exempt, has his firstborn [status] exempt too; and the same for Aaron: though he did not exempt, his firstborn is exempt too.
gershom:a16.1: And this is one of them: of the twenty-four. “But the priests the Levites”: just as here we find explicitly that priests are called Levites, so wherever “Levites” alone is written it also implies the priests.
rashi:b1.1: And for generations, from where do we derive: that the firstborn of priests and Levites are exempt? From this a fortiori inference we learn only about the wilderness.
rashi:b2.1: And from where [is it derived] that it was with a lamb: that the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys were exempted by a Levite’s lamb, as you said above: “a Levite who had a lamb, which abrogated, let [his] be abrogated.”
rashi:b2.2: Silver for generations: regarding the human firstborn (Numbers 18:15–16): “And their redemption money, from a month old you shall redeem, according to your valuation, five shekels of silver.”
rashi:b2.3: Lamb for generations: (Exodus 13:13) “And every firstborn donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.”
rashi:b3.1: With silver they redeemed the firstborn at that time, as it is written (Numbers 3:47): “You shall take five shekels apiece by the poll.”
rashi:b4.1: Consecrated property: (Leviticus 27) “And if he who consecrated it will redeem his house,” etc.; and second tithe, as it is written (Deuteronomy 14): “Then you shall turn it into money.” Therefore they redeemed the firstborn in the wilderness with it, as for later generations. Would you say the same of a lamb, with which consecrated property is not redeemed?
rashi:b6.1: Know: that the firstborn of the Israelites’ animals were not counted [one for one], since the verse did not enumerate a surplus of animals as it enumerated of people: two hundred seventy-three.
rashi:b7.1: Did not have: the Israelites did not have many animals, [compared] with the Levites.
rashi:b8.1: And perhaps even so: although the children of Reuben had a great multitude of livestock, even so the Israelites had no surplus of animals, such that the firstborn of the Israelites’ animals would outnumber the ordinary animals of the Levites.
rashi:b9.1: And say: that what is written, “the animal of the Levites,” means many animals, as we find regarding Nineveh (Jonah 4): “and many animals [uvhema rabba]”; evidently [the singular] behema means many animals.
rashi:b9.2: If so: that behemat of the Levites (and behemtam of the Israelites both) mean many, let the verse write them alike. Since the verse varied its wording, learn from it that one exempted many.
rashi:b10.1: We learn: in the mishna, “and he may redeem with it many times”: if he bought it back from the priest after giving it to him, he redeems another firstborn donkey with it again.
rashi:b10.2: And Rabbi Ḥanina: who said one lamb of a Levite, etc., is explaining the reason of the mishna, and this is what he is saying, etc.
rashi:b11.1: Firstborn were not sanctified: those born in the wilderness.
rashi:b13.1: Initially: in the wilderness. And the verse “Sanctify to Me all the firstborn” Reish Lakish establishes as referring to Egypt; but in the wilderness they were not sanctified, since it is written “when He shall bring you” and then “you shall set apart all that opens the womb.”
rashi:b14.1: Private altars: each person built an altar and sacrificed on it; once the Tabernacle was established they were forbidden, as it is written (Leviticus 17:4): “And has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting,” etc.
rashi:b14.2: And the service by the firstborn: the Israelite firstborn would offer the sacrifices, and from then on the priests. Evidently the firstborn were sanctified.
rashi:b15.1: As if you do not say so: but rather [that it refers] to those born in the wilderness.
rashi:b15.2: Is a one-year-old capable of the service: from when they left Egypt until the Tabernacle was established was only one year.
rashi:b17.1: Did not cease: the sanctity of the firstborn; [if] those born in the wilderness were sanctified, one can say that those born originally [in Egypt; the printed text reads “in the wilderness”] remain in their sanctity, etc.
rashi:b19.1: And from it: one can infer that the firstborn were not sanctified in the wilderness, since it teaches “that day,” by inference that from then on they were not sacrificed: on the first day they sacrificed all the animal firstborn that had left Egypt.
rashi:b21.1: Initially not: each person could not make an altar to sacrifice his own firstborn, since obligatory offerings were not sacrificed on a private altar.
rashi:b23.1: They were commanded to sanctify: and in fact [it took effect only] once they would enter the land.
rashi:b23.2: Were they not sanctified in Egypt: a question of astonishment. Didn’t everyone agree above about those who left Egypt?
rashi:b24.1: But isn’t it written, “Count all the firstborn males”: from a month old and upward; and one a month old was certainly born in the wilderness, since this took place in the second year.
tosafot:b4.1: What is notable about silver, that one redeems consecrated property and second tithe with it: even though consecrated property may be redeemed with a lamb, and with anything except slaves, land and documents, as we say in the chapter Yesh Bekhor (51a below), that is because it is worth money, like money, not because it is a lamb. But a firstborn donkey is redeemed with any lamb at all, and with other things only for their value, as is said below.
tosafot:b10.1: And he may redeem with it many times: Rashi explained: if he bought it back from the priest after giving it to him, he redeems another firstborn donkey with it. Rabbeinu Tam explains that it refers to the doubtful case below in our chapter (9a), whose first clause teaches: one [donkey] had given birth before and one had not, and they bore a male and a female; he sets aside [a lamb], and it is his own. In this doubtful case, where [the lamb] does not leave his possession, it had to teach that he may redeem another doubtful case with it, many times. So too it is implied that it refers to the doubt, since afterward it teaches “it enters the pen to be tithed,” and the Gemara establishes it as a case of doubt. But with a definite [firstborn] one cannot say “he redeems and redeems again” as long as [the lamb] is in the Israelite’s possession and he has not given it, since we learned below in our chapter (9a): two donkeys that had not given birth before bore two males; he gives two lambs to the priest.
tosafot:b11.1: Firstborn were not sanctified in the wilderness: neither the firstborn of man nor the firstborn of an animal. And what was asked above, that they should be exempt even from the firstborn of a kosher animal, since their kosher animals abrogated the Israelites’ kosher animals, is not according to Reish Lakish on his present view. But according to the conclusion below, that they were sanctified [until] the census in the book of Numbers and afterward ceased, it is fine.
tosafot:b19.1: That day: [and] from then on they were not sacrificed. Although vow and gift offerings were sacrificed from then on, it says “that day” because of the firstborn.
tosafot:b24.1: Rather, if it was stated, etc.: according to this conclusion, those refutations above were never said. There are similar cases at the beginning of HaḤoletz (Yevamot 35b) regarding a pregnant widow, in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (7a), and in HaMapelet (Niddah 24a) regarding “its face was smoothed,” and many more in many places.
gershom:b1.1: And for generations, from where do we derive: that firstborn Levites are exempt, as in the wilderness where they exempted? “They shall be in their state.”
gershom:b2.1: And from where [is it derived] that it was with a lamb: that in the wilderness, as it is written “and the animal of the Levites in exchange for the animal,” the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys were redeemed with a lamb? Perhaps they were redeemed with the Levites’ firstborn donkeys. “Silver” is stated for generations: as it is written, “Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem,” and unspecified redemption is with silver.
gershom:b3.1: And “lamb” is stated for generations: as it is written, “you shall redeem with a lamb.”
gershom:b4.1: Just as silver, stated for generations, was used at that time in the wilderness to redeem the firstborn in excess of the Levites, as it is written, “You shall take five shekels apiece by the poll,” etc., so the lamb, stated for generations, was used at that time in the wilderness to redeem the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys. Nevertheless, you cannot learn it by this verbal analogy, since what is notable about silver? It is reasonable that they redeemed with it in the wilderness because it is so significant, in that consecrated property is redeemed with it, etc.
gershom:b5.1: Just as with the firstborn of man you did not distinguish between later generations and that time, since at that time they redeemed the surplus with silver, so with the firstborn of a non-kosher animal, etc. And he learns it from the verse.
gershom:b6.1: And it did not enumerate a surplus of animals among the animal firstborn: learn from this that one lamb exempts several.
gershom:b7.1: And perhaps they did not have many animals: [that is,] more firstborn donkeys than the Levites had sheep. Do not let this enter your mind, since it is written “a very great multitude of livestock”; evidently they had a great many.
gershom:b8.1: And livestock [mikneh]: implies donkeys too, as it is written: “And he carried away all his livestock… the livestock of his getting, which he had gotten” [Genesis 31:18].
gershom:b9.1: And perhaps: although the Israelites had a great deal of livestock, the Levites’ ordinary sheep were many and matched the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys. And it says “ordinary” specifically, since one firstborn does not redeem another firstborn.
gershom:b10.1: And say: what is written, “the animal of the Levites,” from which you want to learn, say it is as written regarding Nineveh, “and many animals,” for this is Scripture’s way of speaking, and it is not one animal.
gershom:b11.1: If so: as you said, let it write either “behemat in exchange for behemat” or “behemtam,” etc.
gershom:b12.1: We too learn: in the mishna, as Rabbi Ḥanina, for we learned: “and he may redeem with it many times.” An Israelite gave a lamb to a priest for the redemption of a firstborn donkey, then the priest gave it back to him, and the Israelite gave it again to the priest for the redemption of another firstborn donkey, and the priest gave it back to the Israelite: he may redeem with that same lamb many times. Evidently one lamb redeems several firstborn donkeys.
gershom:b13.1: And Rabbi Ḥanina: if so, what does he teach us? This he teaches us: he is explaining the reason of the mishna. What is the reason [a gloss suggests: that is why]? Because one lamb exempted several firstborn donkeys (the mishna hangs [its rule] on the lambs), and he learns it from the verse: “the animal of the Levites,” etc.
gershom:b14.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said the firstborn were sanctified in the wilderness: both human firstborn born in the wilderness and animal firstborn born in the wilderness; and all the more so those firstborn that left Egypt, which were sanctified.
gershom:b15.1: And Reish Lakish said the firstborn were not sanctified: [those] born in the wilderness; only those that left Egypt and those born after their entry into the land.
gershom:b16.1: And the service by the firstborn: since it says the service was by the firstborn, evidently the firstborn in the wilderness were sanctified.
gershom:b17.1: He said to him: Reish Lakish [said]: the service was by those firstborn who left Egypt.
gershom:b18.1: This too stands to reason: for if it entered your mind [that it refers] to those born in the wilderness, is a one-year-old capable of performing the service at a private altar? For we hold that in the second year after they left Egypt the Tabernacle was established, the private altars were forbidden, and the service was by the priests.
gershom:b19.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan, he who asked it, why did he ask it? Did he not know that that [mishna] can only be established as referring to those who left Egypt? Yes, but this was Rabbi Yoḥanan’s difficulty: granted, if you say the sanctity of the firstborn never ceased once they were commanded in Egypt, then those original ones born in Egypt remain in their sanctity, and they served at the private altars until the Tabernacle was established.
gershom:b20.1: But if you say the sanctity ceased: that the firstborn were not sanctified all the while they were in the wilderness,
gershom:b21.1: Those original ones too, from Egypt: their sanctity lapsed too; so how was the service by the firstborn?
gershom:b22.1: And the other: Reish Lakish would tell you: those that were sanctified were sanctified. That is, those sanctified in Egypt were sanctified and their sanctity did not lapse afterward, and they served; and those born in the wilderness, which were not sanctified, were not sanctified.
gershom:b23.1: They sacrificed: animal firstborn and tithe; evidently those animal firstborn born in the wilderness were sacrificed, so learn from this that they were sanctified.
gershom:b24.1: And from it: from the baraita itself Reish Lakish answers Rabbi Yoḥanan: since it teaches “that day they sacrificed vows… and firstborn,” it was that day that firstborn were sacrificed, and from then on not. Must we not learn from this, since they were not sacrificed from then on, that the firstborn were not sanctified in the wilderness, and those that were sacrificed were those that left Egypt?
gershom:b25.1: Some say: the reverse: Reish Lakish raised an objection to Rabbi Yoḥanan: “that day,” etc. That day yes, from then on no, because the firstborn were not sanctified in the wilderness. [And what does it teach us?] That day they sacrificed sin offerings and guilt offerings; initially not. Evidently obligatory offerings, such as sin offerings and guilt offerings, were not sacrificed at a private altar, even a public one, as it says: this is the principle, whatever is vowed or donated is sacrificed at a private altar, such as vow and gift offerings; but in the Tabernacle obligatory offerings were sacrificed, that day and from then on.
gershom:b26.1: Come and hear, “you are found to be saying”: with this baraita Rabbi Yoḥanan raises an objection to Reish Lakish.
gershom:b27.1: In three locations: they were commanded to sanctify the firstborn: in Egypt, and in the wilderness, etc.
gershom:b28.1: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: he answers according to Rabbi Shimon [ben Lakish]: in three locations they were commanded regarding the firstborn to sanctify them, but they did not sanctify. Even so, did they not sanctify in all three locations? That is, [if] in the wilderness they did not sanctify, then in Egypt too were they not sanctified?
gershom:b29.1: But we said that they were sanctified: since firstborn and tithes were sacrificed. [This is what it is saying:] that they were sanctified.
gershom:b30.1: Of some they sanctified and of some they did not: those of Egypt were sanctified, and in the wilderness they were not sanctified, since they were not commanded.
gershom:b31.1: And in the wilderness were they not sanctified? But isn’t it written “Count,” etc. Rabbi Yoḥanan says the firstborn were sanctified in the wilderness and the sanctity did not cease; and Reish Lakish says [they were sanctified and ceased]: even though “Count” is written, [nevertheless] they were sanctified and then ceased.
